transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

I'm really struggling with how awful my skin looks, and it's making me feel incredibly self-conscious. My face is just completely ruined by these terrible acne scars and breakouts, and I can't stop worrying about it. I feel so anxious just being seen like this.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time—more than an hour a day—thinking about or trying to fix your skin, even when others might not notice anything wrong?

Yes, I easily spend two or three hours every day picking at any tiny bump I find and trying to cover everything up with makeup. My family constantly tells me they can't even see anything wrong, but to me, the flaws look absolutely terrible and I just can't leave them alone.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or lost interest in things you used to enjoy, even when you're not focusing on your skin?
No, I don't really feel hopeless or lose interest in things in general. It's just that my skin looks so awful that it completely takes over my mind and makes it hard to focus on anything else.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["Body Dysmorphic Disorder", "Generalized Anxiety Disorder", "Major Depressive Disorder"], but based on this conversation, Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Major Depressive Disorder are less likely because the patient's distress is specifically tied to a preoccupation with perceived defects in appearance (skin) rather than generalized worry or pervasive low mood. The patient spends excessive time on appearance-related behaviors (picking, camouflaging), has insight that others don't see the flaws, yet remains preoccupied — which is characteristic of Body Dysmorphic Disorder. The absence of anhedonia or hopelessness argues against Major Depressive Disorder. Thus, the current candidate is narrowed to Body Dysmorphic Disorder.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits excessive preoccupation with perceived defects in appearance (skin and acne scars) not observable to others, spends significant time (2–3 hours daily) on repetitive behaviors (picking, covering with makeup), and experiences marked distress, all hallmark features of Body Dysmorphic Disorder. No evidence of depressed mood or anhedonia outside appearance concerns, reducing likelihood of Major Depressive Disorder. OCD is considered due to compulsive behaviors but focus remains on appearance preoccupation, supporting BDD as primary diagnosis.
